title: The kings of Assyria and Babylon

intro.text: Nine kings of Assyria and Babylon have pages here: five of Assyria (Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sargon, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon) and four of Babylon (Merodach-baladan, Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-merodach, Belshazzar). Scripture names each of them, but gives none a regnal formula, a length of reign or a verdict; each page quotes what Scripture says of him and adds no judgement.

Scripture dates no event by the years of an Assyrian king. With Nebuchadnezzar that changes: Kings and Jeremiah date events by his years, from his first to his twenty-third, Jehoiachin's release by the year Evil-merodach began to reign, and Daniel's visions by Belshazzar's years.

These kings, or their scribes, also left records that name kings of Israel and Judah: Menahem, Pekah, Hoshea, Ahaz (as "Jehoahaz"), Hezekiah and Manasseh appear in Assyrian annals and lists, and Jehoiachin in Babylonian ration tablets. The pages show Scripture and these records side by side without merging them, and say what each record leaves out.

Their dates come from their own records, not from Scripture: the Assyrian eponym lists, the Babylonian Chronicle and king lists, and Ptolemy's canon. The main dates shown are Luckenbill's (1926–27) for Assyria and Dougherty's (1929) for Babylon; Rogers (1912) and Driver (1900) differ from them by a year here and there.

rulers.name: Tiglath-pileser
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.tagline: The Assyrian king who took Galilee and Gilead, and to whom Ahaz sent the temple's silver.

capital.name: Calah (Nimrud)
capital.note: His annals were carved on the slabs of his rebuilt palace at Calah (Luckenbill 1926, §761). Scripture names no capital for him.

identifications.text: This page treats "Pul the king of Assyria" (2 Kings 15:19) as Tiglath-pileser, as the site's person data does. Rogers (1912) gives the reason: the king took the name Tiglath-pileser in Assyria and was known as Pulu in Babylonia. It is an identification, not Scripture's own statement; the views are set out below.
Chronicles spells the name Tilgath-pilneser; Kings spells it Tiglath-pileser.
The site's person data also files "king Jareb" (Hosea 5:13; 10:6) under this king. That too is an identification; see the question below.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign. It places him in the days of Menahem, Pekah and Ahaz.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives no year or length of his reign; it dates him by the kings of Israel and Judah (2 Kgs 15:19; 15:29; 16:7).

dates.label: Rogers (1912)
dates.note: Rogers numbers him Tiglathpileser IV, an older numbering.

dates.label: Babylonian king lists
dates.note: As king of Babylon: "Pulu", two years, in the Babylonian king list; Chinzer and Poros, five years from 731 BC, in Ptolemy's canon (Rogers's tables).

scriptureSays.text: "Pul the king of Assyria came against the land" in Menahem's reign; Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver, "that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand", and "the king of Assyria turned back".

"In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria", took Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee and "all the land of Naphtali", and carried the people captive to Assyria.
Ahaz of Judah sent to him: "I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me". He went up against Damascus, took it, carried its people captive to Kir and slew Rezin.
Chronicles: "Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came unto him, and distressed him, but strengthened him not."

Chronicles: "the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria", and the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh were carried to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan.

claim.text: "Pul the king of Assyria came against the land"; Menahem raised a thousand talents of silver, fifty shekels from each man of wealth, and the king of Assyria turned back.
In Pekah's days he took Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee and all the land of Naphtali, and carried the people to Assyria.

events.label: The tribes beyond Jordan carried away

claim.text: He carried away the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan; Beerah, prince of the Reubenites, was among the captives.
Besieged by Rezin and Pekah, Ahaz sent messengers and a present of silver and gold from the temple and the palace treasuries.
"The king of Assyria went up against Damascus, and took it, and carried the people of it captive to Kir, and slew Rezin."
King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser, saw an altar there, and sent its pattern to Urijah the priest, who built a copy in Jerusalem.

events.label: Changes made "for the king of Assyria"

claim.text: Ahaz cut off the borders of the bases, took the sea down from the brasen oxen, and turned the covert for the sabbath and the king's entry from the house of the LORD "for the king of Assyria".
Chronicles: Ahaz gave him a portion out of the house of the LORD, the king's house and the princes', "but he helped him not".

worship.text: The altar Ahaz saw at Damascus, when he went to meet Tiglath-pileser, was copied in Jerusalem; Ahaz moved the brasen altar aside and kept it "for me to enquire by".

alliances.text: Menahem paid a thousand talents of silver "to confirm the kingdom in his hand".
Ahaz called himself "thy servant and thy son" and sent the silver and gold of the temple and the palace.
Chronicles: he "distressed him, but strengthened him not".

people.text: Menahem raised the money from "all the mighty men of wealth, of each man fifty shekels of silver".
The people of Naphtali, Gilead and Galilee were carried captive to Assyria.
The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh were carried away "unto this day".
The people of Damascus were carried captive to Kir.

claim.text: In the days of Ahaz, Isaiah said the LORD would bring "the king of Assyria" on Judah, and that "the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria" would be taken away before him. Isaiah does not name the king; Kings names Tiglath-pileser as the king of Assyria to whom Ahaz appealed.

quote.text: the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of Assyria

claim.text: Hosea said that Ephraim went "to the Assyrian" and sent "to king Jareb", who could not heal them; and that the calf of Beth-aven would be "carried unto Assyria for a present to king Jareb". Who king Jareb is, is a question set out below.

quote.text: then went Ephraim to the Assyrian, and sent to king Jareb: yet could he not heal you, nor cure you of your wound.

claim.text: Menahem paid him tribute; in Pekah's days he took the north and Gilead.
Ahaz appealed to him for help against Rezin and Pekah and went to meet him at Damascus.
He took Damascus and slew Rezin.

A list of kings who paid him tribute names "Menihimmu (Menahem) of Samerina (Samaria)", beside "Rasunnu (Rezin) of Aram" and Hiram of Tyre (Luckenbill's translation; Rogers's translation also names Menahem of Samaria). It gives one list of goods for all the kings together, so it does not say what Menahem paid.

outside.name: Fragmentary annals: Naphtali, Gaza and Samaria

claim.text: A broken text says he brought "the wide land of Naphtali, in its entirety" within the border of Assyria and set his own official over it, and that Hanno of Gaza fled to Egypt. A damaged line reads, with Luckenbill's own question mark: "As for Menahem(?), terror overwhelmed him, like a bird, alone he fled and submitted to me."

The same text says: "Pakaha, their king they deposed and I placed Ausi' (Hoshea) over them as king", and that he received 10 talents of gold from them (Luckenbill); Rogers: "As Pekah, their king, they had deposed, Hosea I established as king over them." Kings tells it otherwise: Hoshea conspired against Pekah and slew him, and reigned in his stead.

His annals tell of the siege of "Hadaru, the father's house of Resin of Aram" and of "591 cities of 16 districts of Aram" laid waste; the eponym list notes campaigns "against the land of Damascus" in 733 and 732. In Luckenbill's translation the surviving pieces do not describe the taking of Damascus or Rezin's death, which Kings records.

A list of kings who brought him tribute includes "Iauhazi (Jehoahaz) of Judah", the full form of Ahaz's name. Rogers notes it is the first mention of Judah in the Assyrian inscriptions. It says nothing of Ahaz's appeal or of the altar at Damascus.

"In the third year of Nabonassar, King of Babylon, Tiglathpileser took his seat on the throne in Assyria." Later he took the throne in Babylon himself; the chronicle says "two years he reigned in Akkad", and that he died in the month Tebet.

outside.name: Babylonian king list and Ptolemy's canon
outside.date: copied centuries later (the canon is Greek)

claim.text: The Babylonian king list names a king "Pulu" for two years, followed by "Ululai" for five. Ptolemy's canon has Chinzer and Poros (Greek forms that Rogers sets beside Ukinzer and Pulu) for five years from 731 BC. Neither list uses the name Tiglath-pileser.

first.text: Kings: "Pul the king of Assyria" in Menahem's reign, and "Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria" in Pekah's.

second.text: Chronicles: "the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away": two names, one verb.

first.text: Kings: "the king of Assyria hearkened unto him", took Damascus and slew Rezin.

second.text: Chronicles: he "distressed him, but strengthened him not"; "he helped him not".

questions.question: Is "Pul" the same king as Tiglath-pileser?

views.label: One king: Pul was his name in Babylon
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912); Ellicott's commentary (about 1880); W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: Rogers: the new king "was proclaimed under the name and style of Tiglathpileser in Assyria, and later under the name of Pulu in Babylonia". The Babylonian king list has a "Pulu" reigning two years where the Babylonian Chronicle puts Tiglath-pileser on Babylon's throne for two years. Ellicott's commentary: "Pûl appears to have been the original name of Tiglath-pileser"; Barnes takes Pul as the earlier name and Tiglath-pileser as the royal name of one king.

views.label: Two kings, as the KJV wording reads
views.holders: John Gill (1748–63); C. F. Keil (1872); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Gill takes Pul as the king of Menahem's day and Tilgath-pilneser as the king of Pekah's day, the one who carried the tribes away. Keil speaks of "the Assyrian kings Pul and Tiglath-pilneser"; the Pulpit Commentary also treats them as two.

views.label: How translations render the verse
views.holders: the KJV and the World English Bible; the Berean Standard Bible

argument.text: The KJV reads "and the spirit of Tilgath-pilneser", and the WEB likewise ("Tilgath Pilneser"). The Berean Standard Bible (BSB, a modern translation on this site, public domain since 2023) reads "Pul king of Assyria (that is, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria)".

views.label: The Assyrian king of the day
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–85); the site's person data

argument.text: Poole holds that whichever king of Assyria Ephraim and Judah turned to is meant: "Pul in Menahem's time, Tiglath-pileser in Ahaz's time". The site's person data files both verses under Tiglath-pileser.

views.label: A title, not a name
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868); T. K. Cheyne (1884); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Keil renders "king Jareb (striver)"; Cheyne calls it "a nickname for the king of Assyria", "the fighting king"; the Pulpit Commentary reads it as an epithet for a warlike or champion king.

views.label: An earlier Assyrian king
views.holders: E. Schrader, as reported by T. K. Cheyne (1884)

argument.text: Schrader thought the king meant was Asurdan (Asshur-dan), who campaigned in the west in 755 and 754 BC.

notSaid: Scripture gives no year or length for Tiglath-pileser's reign and does not say how he died.
Kings does not say that Tiglath-pileser set Hoshea on Israel's throne; that is in his own annals.
Scripture does not mention his reign in Babylon.
Isaiah names no king of Assyria in his words to Ahaz.

places.name: Calah (Nimrud)
places.note: His palace and annals (not in Scripture's account of him)

places.name: Kir
places.note: Where the people of Damascus were taken

rulers.name: Shalmaneser
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.tagline: The king of Assyria who made Hoshea his servant and besieged Samaria.

capital.name: Assyria
capital.note: Scripture names his kingdom, not a capital city.

identifications.text: Kings does not number him; historians call him Shalmaneser V, to tell him from earlier kings of the name.
The site's person record for him also holds "Shalman" (Hosea 10:14). Whether Hosea meant this king is a question set out below.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign. It places him in the reigns of Hoshea of Israel and Hezekiah of Judah.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives no year of his own reign; it dates the siege of Samaria to Hoshea's 7th–9th years and Hezekiah's 4th–6th (2 Kgs 18:9–10).

dates.label: Rogers (1912)
dates.note: Tiglath-pileser died in Tebet 727; Shalmaneser V died in 722.

dates.label: The Babylonian Chronicle
dates.note: "Shalmaneser reigned five years in Akkad and in Assyria." In the same place the Babylonian king list and Ptolemy's canon have a king "Ululai" for five years.

scriptureSays.text: "Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria; and Hoshea became his servant, and gave him presents."
When Hoshea sent messengers to So king of Egypt and brought no present "as he had done year by year", "the king of Assyria shut him up, and bound him in prison".
"Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria, and besieged it. And at the end of three years they took it."
Kings does not name the king who took Samaria: 2 Kings 17:6 says "the king of Assyria took Samaria", and 2 Kings 18:10 "they took it".

quote.text: in the fourth year of king Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, that Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria, and besieged it.

claim.text: Shalmaneser came up against Hoshea, and Hoshea became his servant and paid him presents year by year.
Finding that Hoshea had sent to So king of Egypt and withheld his present, the king of Assyria shut him up and bound him in prison.
Kings: "the king of Assyria came up throughout all the land" and besieged Samaria three years; 2 Kings 18:9 names Shalmaneser and dates the start to Hoshea's seventh year.
"At the end of three years they took it": Hoshea's ninth year, Hezekiah's sixth.
"The king of Assyria" carried Israel away to Halah, to Habor by the river of Gozan, and to the cities of the Medes. Kings does not name the king here.

worship.text: Kings gives the reason for Samaria's fall: "Because they obeyed not the voice of the LORD their God, but transgressed his covenant".

alliances.text: Hoshea paid him presents "year by year" until he turned to So king of Egypt.

people.text: Samaria endured a three-year siege, and Israel was carried away into Assyria.

claim.text: Hosea warned that Israel's fortresses would be spoiled "as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in the day of battle". Whether Shalman is this king is a question set out below.

quote.text: all thy fortresses shall be spoiled, as Shalman spoiled Beth-arbel in the day of battle

claim.text: Hoshea became his servant, then sought help from Egypt and was imprisoned.
Hoshea "had sent messengers to So king of Egypt".
Kings dates the siege of Samaria by Hezekiah's years.
For 727 the list notes "Shalmaneser took his seat on the throne"; for 725, 724 and 723 it records campaigns "against [Samaria]". The place name is broken and was restored by the editor, Luckenbill.

On the twenty-fifth of Tebet Shalmaneser took the throne of Assyria "and the city of Shabarain was destroyed" (Rogers's translation); in Tebet of his fifth year he died, having "reigned five years in Akkad and in Assyria".
Luckenbill knew only one text of Shalmaneser V himself: a badly broken memorial cylinder from Nabu's temple at Borsippa. In what can be read, no place in Israel is named.
Sargon, the next king, claims that in the beginning of his reign he besieged and took Samaria and carried off 27,290 people.

questions.question: Who took Samaria: Shalmaneser or Sargon?

argument.text: Kings names Shalmaneser as the king who besieged Samaria and says "at the end of three years they took it", without naming the king who took it.
Grayson's edition of the Babylonian Chronicle reads that Shalmaneser ravaged Samaria at the start of his reign. Rogers (1912) printed the name as "Shabarain" without placing it.
Sargon lists the capture of Samaria among his deeds "from the year of my accession to the fifteenth year of my reign" (Luckenbill).

Rogers: Samaria fell in 722, immediately on Shalmaneser's death; "Sargon claims the victory for himself, though he could not have been present at all", and the city "may have fallen while Shalmaneser still lived".

views.label: Yes, a shortened form of his name
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–85); John Gill (1748–63); C. F. Keil (1868); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Poole and Gill take Shalman as Shalmaneser's name shortened, and Keil as a contracted form of it. The Pulpit Commentary, admitting "a certain chronological difficulty", places the sack of Beth-arbel in the campaign of 2 Kings 17:3–5.

views.label: Uncertain: an earlier king, or Salamanu of Moab
views.holders: E. Schrader, as reported by T. K. Cheyne (1884)

argument.text: Cheyne: "Who Shalman was, is altogether uncertain." He reports Schrader's two suggestions: an earlier Shalmaneser who campaigned in the west in 775–773 BC, or a Moabite king Salamanu named by Tiglath-pileser as his tributary. Ellicott's commentary calls the Moabite theory "far-fetched and improbable".

views.label: Zalmunna of Midian
views.holders: the Septuagint, the Old Latin and the Vulgate, followed by Bishop Horsley and Abraham Geiger (as reported by T. K. Cheyne, 1884)

argument.text: Several ancient versions read a reference to Zalmunna, the Midianite king slain by Gideon.

notSaid: Scripture gives no length for Shalmaneser's reign and does not say how he died.
Kings does not say which king of Assyria was on the throne when Samaria fell.
Scripture does not say what became of Hoshea after he was bound in prison.

places.name: Beth-arbel
places.note: If Hosea's Shalman is this king

rulers.name: Sargon
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.tagline: Named once in Scripture: the king who sent his Tartan against Ashdod.

capital.name: Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad)
capital.note: Rogers (1912): the new city he "had built for his future residence", dedicated in 706 BC. Scripture names no capital for him.

identifications.text: Scripture names Sargon only in Isaiah 20:1. Older writers often took the name for another name of Sennacherib or of another king; the Assyrian records show him as a king in his own right, the father of Sennacherib (see the question below).

"Tartan" is a title, the Assyrian commander next to the king. The site's person record for Tartan joins the Tartan of Isaiah 20:1 with Sennacherib's Tartan (2 Kings 18:17); Ellicott's commentary says the two "may, or may not" be the same man.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign and dates nothing by it.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: Scripture names Sargon once and gives no dates for him (Isa 20:1).

dates.label: The Babylonian Chronicle and eponym list
dates.note: He took the throne on the twelfth of Tebet after Shalmaneser's death; Sennacherib took the throne on the twelfth of Ab, 705 BC.

scriptureSays.text: "In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it".

At that time the LORD told Isaiah to loose the sackcloth from his loins and put off his shoes, "walking naked and barefoot", as a sign that "the king of Assyria" would lead the Egyptians and the Ethiopians away captive.

claim.text: Sargon sent the Tartan to Ashdod; he fought against it and took it.
Isaiah walked naked and barefoot three years "for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia".

alliances.text: The sign was aimed at those who looked to Ethiopia and Egypt for help: "such is our expectation, whither we flee for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria".

claim.text: In the year of the Ashdod campaign Isaiah walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign that the king of Assyria would lead Egypt's and Ethiopia's people away captive.

quote.text: So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot

claim.text: Ashdod, a Philistine city, was fought against and taken.
Isaiah's sign foretold that the king of Assyria would lead Egyptians and Ethiopians away captive.

outside.name: Sargon's annals: Samaria
outside.date: his first year (722–721 BC by Rogers)

claim.text: Sargon says that at the beginning of his rule he carried away 27,290 people of Samaria and took 50 chariots; that he rebuilt the city and made it greater than before; and that he settled there people of lands he had conquered and set his official over them as governor.

His annals add that he deported desert Arab tribes and "settled them in Samaria". Kings says that "the king of Assyria" brought men from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim to the cities of Samaria, without naming him.

In his eleventh year, Sargon says, Azuru king of Ashdod withheld tribute; Sargon put Azuru's brother in his place; the people set up Iamani instead; and Sargon "advanced in haste" with his own chariots and horsemen, took Ashdod, Gath and Asdudimmu, and set his official over them as governor. A prism fragment adds that the rebels sent messages to the kings of "Piliste (Philistia), Iaudi (Judah), Edom, Moab" (Edom partly restored) and presents to "Pir'u, king of Egypt".

outside.name: What the Ashdod records do not say

claim.text: They do not mention the Tartan or name any king of Judah, and they do not say that Judah joined the revolt. The prism fragment dates the campaign to the ninth year of the reign, the annals to the eleventh (Rogers's note).
An inscription from Nimrud calls Sargon "subduer of the land of Iaudu (Judah), which lies far away". It names no king of Judah and gives no occasion.
The eponym list for 705 BC is broken around the words "the camp of the King of Assyria", and records that on the twelfth of Ab "Sennacherib took his seat on the throne".

views.label: Another name of Sennacherib
views.holders: the Geneva Bible notes (1599); John Gill (1748–63)

argument.text: The Geneva note says "The Hebrews write that Sennacherib was so called". Gill: Sargon "is generally thought to be the same with Sennacherib, since Tartan was one of his generals" (2 Kings 18:17).
Poole, noting that kings often had several names, offers three candidates: Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, or Esarhaddon, whose name he thought might be shortened to Sargon.

views.label: A king of his own, Sennacherib's father

argument.text: Skinner: the guess of a few scholars that Sargon was "an intermediate king" had been "amply verified by the progress of Assyriology"; he reigned 722–705. Rogers writes that Sennacherib, Sargon's son, took the throne in the month Sargon died.

questions.question: Did Sargon send his Tartan to Ashdod, or go himself?

argument.text: "Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,)".

views.label: Sargon's annals: the king went himself

argument.text: The annals say Sargon advanced on Ashdod "in haste" with his war chariot and the horsemen "who never depart from my side".
Ashdod was besieged twice under Sargon, in 713 and 711 BC: the first time probably by a general (the Tartan), the second by Sargon in person. Isaiah 20:1 refers to the first.

notSaid: Scripture names Sargon once and records nothing else he did.
Isaiah 20 does not say whether Judah joined Ashdod's revolt.
Scripture does not connect Sargon with the fall of Samaria; that claim is in his own inscriptions.
Scripture does not say how Sargon died.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: Named in his own annals, not in Scripture's account of him

rulers.name: Sennacherib
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.tagline: The king of Assyria who took Judah's fenced cities and sent his army against Jerusalem, then went home to Nineveh.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign. It dates his invasion to Hezekiah's fourteenth year.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: His invasion came "in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah" (2 Kgs 18:13; Isa 36:1); Scripture gives no year of his own reign.

dates.label: The Babylonian Chronicle
dates.note: "Sennacherib reigned twenty-three years in Assyria"; he was killed on the twentieth of Tebet. Polyhistor, quoted by Eusebius, gives eighteen years.

scriptureSays.text: "Now in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah did Sennacherib king of Assyria come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them."
At Lachish he appointed Hezekiah "three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold".
He sent Tartan, Rabsaris and Rab-shakeh with a great host against Jerusalem, and then a letter: "Let not thy God in whom thou trustest deceive thee".

"The angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand"; "So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh."
Worshipping "in the house of Nisroch his god", he was struck down with the sword by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer, who escaped into Armenia.
Chronicles: "he returned with shame of face to his own land".

quote.text: Now in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah did Sennacherib king of Assyria come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them.

claim.text: Kings and Isaiah: he came up against all the fenced cities of Judah and took them. Chronicles: he encamped against them, and "thought to win them for himself".
Hezekiah sent to him at Lachish, "I have offended", and paid 300 talents of silver and 30 of gold, stripping gold from the temple doors.
His officers spoke to Jerusalem from the conduit of the upper pool, in the Jews' language, mocking Judah's trust in the LORD and in Egypt.
Rab-shakeh found him warring against Libnah; hearing that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia was coming out to fight, he sent a letter to Hezekiah.
His letter reminded Hezekiah what "the kings of Assyria have done to all lands"; Chronicles says he wrote "letters to rail on the LORD God of Israel".
Kings and Isaiah: the angel of the LORD smote 185,000 in the Assyrian camp in one night. Chronicles: an angel cut off the mighty men of valour and the captains, and gives no number.
He departed, returned and dwelt at Nineveh.
As he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons killed him with the sword and fled to Armenia; Esar-haddon his son reigned in his stead.

worship.text: Rab-shakeh claimed "The LORD said to me, Go up against this land, and destroy it", and pointed to the high places and altars Hezekiah had taken away.
Hezekiah spread Sennacherib's letter before the LORD in the temple and prayed.

alliances.text: He took Hezekiah's tribute of silver and gold.
Rab-shakeh called Egypt "this bruised reed" and offered terms: "Make an agreement with me by a present".

people.text: Rab-shakeh promised to take the people "to a land like your own land"; "the people held their peace, and answered him not a word".
Chronicles: afterwards "many brought gifts unto the LORD to Jerusalem, and presents to Hezekiah".

claim.text: Isaiah told Hezekiah not to fear: Sennacherib would hear a rumour, return to his own land and fall by the sword there. He answered Hezekiah's prayer with a word "concerning him": the daughter of Zion had laughed him to scorn, and the LORD would put a hook in his nose and turn him back.

quote.text: He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor cast a bank against it.

claim.text: Hezekiah paid tribute, then prayed when Sennacherib's officers and letter came.
Rab-shakeh mocked trust in "Pharaoh king of Egypt"; news that Tirhakah had come out to fight made Sennacherib send his letter.
Two of his sons killed him; Esar-haddon his son reigned in his stead.

"As for Hezekiah, the Jew, who did not submit to my yoke, 46 of his strong, walled cities" were besieged and taken and 200,150 people carried off; "Himself, like a caged bird I shut up in Jerusalem his royal city." Hezekiah later sent 30 talents of gold and 800 talents of silver after him to Nineveh. (Taylor Prism, British Museum 91032; Oriental Institute Prism, Chicago A2793.)

outside.name: What the annals do not say

claim.text: The annals never claim that Jerusalem was taken, and say nothing of a disaster to the Assyrian army. They agree with Kings on 30 talents of gold; Kings gives 300 talents of silver, the annals 800. Luckenbill noted that the annals do not mention Sennacherib's presence before Lachish.

Carved panels from his palace at Nineveh show the siege of Lachish, with the caption: "Sennacherib, king of the universe, king of Assyria, sat upon a throne (lit. standing-chair) (while) the booty of Lachish passed before him" (Luckenbill, 1924, p. 156). They do not name Hezekiah or Jerusalem.
The same annals tell how he defeated Merodach-baladan of Babylon "in the plain of Kish" and later drove him to flee by ship, and how he set his eldest son, Assur-nadin-shum, on Babylon's throne.

outside.name: The Babylonian Chronicle on his death

claim.text: "On the twentieth day of Tebet Sennacherib, King of Assyria, was killed by his son in a revolt. Sennacherib reigned twenty-three years in Assyria." The revolt lasted until the second of Adar; on the eighteenth of Adar Esarhaddon his son took the throne.

Esarhaddon writes that his brothers plotted against him and, in a passage partly restored by Luckenbill, "slew Sennacherib, their father"; that he marched on Nineveh in winter; and that the instigators of the revolt "fled to parts unknown".

Herodotus tells an Egyptian story that when "Sanacharib king of the Arabians and of the Assyrians" marched against Egypt, field mice gnawed his army's quivers and bows by night at Pelusium. He does not mention Judah, Jerusalem or Hezekiah.

outside.name: Polyhistor and Abydenus
outside.date: Greek writers of the 1st century BC and later, quoted by Eusebius

claim.text: Polyhistor says Sennacherib "remained in power eighteen years and died by the hand of his son Ardumuzanus, in an uprising"; Abydenus, in a confused order of kings, has a king "Nergilus" cut off by his son "Adramelus", who was killed in turn by his brother "Axerdis" (Rogers's translations).

first.text: Kings: he came "against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them"; Isaiah says the same.

second.text: Chronicles: he "encamped against the fenced cities, and thought to win them for himself"; it does not say he took them.

first.text: Kings: Hezekiah sent to Lachish, "I have offended", and paid 300 talents of silver and 30 of gold.

second.text: Chronicles does not mention the tribute.

first.text: Kings: the angel of the LORD smote "an hundred fourscore and five thousand".

second.text: Chronicles: an angel "cut off all the mighty men of valour, and the leaders and captains"; it gives no number.

first.text: Kings: his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer smote him "as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god", and fled to Armenia.

second.text: Chronicles: "when he was come into the house of his god, they that came forth of his own bowels slew him there with the sword"; it names no son.

questions.question: How did Sennacherib's campaign against Judah end?

argument.text: The angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib went home; Isaiah had said he would not come into the city.

views.label: Sennacherib's account
views.holders: Sennacherib's annals (translated by D. D. Luckenbill, 1924)

argument.text: A blockade, Hezekiah's submission, and tribute sent after Sennacherib to Nineveh; no defeat is mentioned.

views.label: A victory that was not decisive

argument.text: Luckenbill judged the very full account of the siege "a sure sign that the victory claimed was not at all decisive".
Herodotus heard in Egypt that Sanacharib's army at Pelusium lost its bows and quivers to field mice in one night and fled. He sets the story in Egypt, not Judah.
"Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword".
The chronicle says he "was killed by his son in a revolt", naming no son.
Esarhaddon blames his brothers; the line naming the killing is partly restored by the editor.
Polyhistor names the son "Ardumuzanus". Abydenus, whose order of kings is confused, has "Adramelus" kill a king he calls Nergilus.

notSaid: Scripture does not say how long Sennacherib lived after he returned to Nineveh.
Scripture does not say how the 185,000 in the Assyrian camp died.
Scripture does not name Sennacherib's father.
Scripture does not say where the house of Nisroch his god stood.

places.name: Lachish
places.note: His camp; Hezekiah's tribute sent there

rulers.name: Esarhaddon
rulers.title: King of Assyria
rulers.tagline: Sennacherib's son, who reigned after him; settlers he brought into the land dated their worship from his days.

capital.name: Nineveh
capital.note: He entered Nineveh to take his father's throne (Luckenbill 1927, §506).

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign; it says only that he reigned in his father's stead.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives no years for him (2 Kgs 19:37; Ezra 4:2).

dates.label: The Babylonian Chronicle
dates.note: After Sennacherib's murder on the twentieth of Tebet, the revolt lasted until the second of Adar; Esarhaddon took the throne on the eighteenth of Adar.

scriptureSays.text: "And Esar-haddon his son reigned in his stead."
The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin told Zerubbabel: "we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esar-haddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither."

claim.text: When Adrammelech and Sharezer killed Sennacherib and fled, Esar-haddon reigned in his stead.
The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin said Esar-haddon had brought them to the land.

worship.text: The settlers said they had sacrificed to Israel's God "since the days of Esar-haddon"; Zerubbabel and Jeshua refused their help with the temple.

alliances.text: Chronicles says "the captains of the host of the king of Assyria" took Manasseh to Babylon, but does not name the king; see the question below.

people.text: Three passages speak of foreigners settled in Samaria: 2 Kings 17:24 ("the king of Assyria", unnamed), Ezra 4:2 (Esar-haddon) and Ezra 4:10 ("the great and noble Asnappar").

claim.text: His brothers killed their father Sennacherib and fled into Armenia.
Esarhaddon names "Manasseh, king of Judah" among the kings who brought him building materials.
His stele from Senjirli says he took Memphis and wounded "Tirhakah, king of Egypt and Ethiopia (Kush)" five times.

Chosen as heir by his father, he says, he was opposed by his brothers, who revolted and (in a partly restored line) slew Sennacherib; he hurried to Nineveh in the cold of Shabatu, the rebels' troops came over to him, the instigators "fled to parts unknown", and in Adar he "took my seat upon the throne of my father".

Sennacherib was killed "by his son in a revolt" on the twentieth of Tebet; the revolt continued until the second of Adar; "On the eighteenth day of Adar Esarhaddon, his son, took his seat on the throne in Assyria." In his tenth year the chronicle records three battles in Egypt and the capture of Memphis, "its royal city".

For his palace at Nineveh he summoned twenty-two kings of the west and of Cyprus to bring timber and stone; the list includes "Manasseh, king of Judah" (Me-na-si-e), second after Ba'al of Tyre. It says nothing of a captivity in Babylon.
"Memphis, his royal city, in half a day, with mines, tunnels, assaults, I besieged, I captured": the stele boasts of the defeat of Tirhakah, the king named in 2 Kings 19:9.

questions.question: Which king of Assyria took Manasseh to Babylon (2 Chronicles 33:11)?

argument.text: "The captains of the host of the king of Assyria, which took Manasseh among the thorns, and bound him with fetters, and carried him to Babylon."

views.label: Esarhaddon
views.holders: John Gill (1748–63); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Gill and Jamieson–Fausset–Brown name Esar-haddon; the Pulpit Commentary prefers Esarhaddon and thinks his son Assur-banipal less likely.

views.label: Asshur-bani-pal, his son
views.holders: W. E. Barnes (1899); Ellicott's commentary (about 1880), tentatively

argument.text: Barnes points to a great revolt against Asshur-bani-pal in which Western Asia, "and perhaps Manasseh", was involved; Ellicott's commentary says Esarhaddon's generals, "or rather, perhaps, of Assurbanipal".

views.label: The records are silent
views.holders: the lists of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal

argument.text: Both kings list Manasseh among their vassals; neither mentions a captivity.

notSaid: Scripture records no campaign of Esarhaddon against Israel or Judah.
Scripture gives no length for his reign and does not say how he died.
Ezra 4:2 does not say where the settlers came from.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: "the cities of Samaria", where Asnappar set nations; Ezra 4:2 names no place

places.name: Memphis
places.note: Taken, by his own stele and the Babylonian Chronicle (not in Scripture)

rulers.name: Merodach-baladan
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.tagline: The king of Babylon whose envoys Hezekiah showed all his treasures.

identifications.text: Kings spells his name Berodach-baladan and Isaiah Merodach-baladan; both call him "the son of Baladan, king of Babylon".
He is the Marduk-apal-iddina (Merodach-baladan) of the Assyrian and Babylonian records, as Luckenbill's and Rogers's translations render the name.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign. It sets his embassy "at that time", after Hezekiah's illness.

dates.label: Rogers (1912)
dates.note: Proclaimed king at the New Year of 721 BC; twelve years, until Sargon drove him out. A second reign of nine months by the Babylonian king list, which Rogers places in 702 BC.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: Scripture gives no years for him (2 Kgs 20:12; Isa 39:1).

dates.label: Ptolemy's canon
dates.note: Twelve years from 721 BC (Rogers's table).

dates.label: Lumby (1887)
dates.note: Driven out in 709 BC; back on the throne in 702 BC for a brief time.

scriptureSays.text: "At that time Berodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a present unto Hezekiah: for he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick."
Isaiah's account: "he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered".
Chronicles speaks of "the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent unto him to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land".

claim.text: He sent letters and a present to Hezekiah when he heard of his sickness.
Hezekiah showed his envoys "all the house of his precious things" and his armour: "there was nothing in his house, nor in all his dominion, that Hezekiah shewed them not".
Isaiah told Hezekiah that all his treasures would be carried to Babylon and some of his sons made eunuchs "in the palace of the king of Babylon".

worship.text: Chronicles: in the business of the ambassadors "God left him, to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart".

alliances.text: Letters and a present for Hezekiah; Hezekiah "hearkened unto them" (Kings) or "was glad of them" (Isaiah).

people.text: Isaiah foretold that some of Hezekiah's own sons would serve as eunuchs in the king of Babylon's palace.

claim.text: Isaiah asked Hezekiah where the men had come from and what they had seen, then gave the word of the LORD that everything would be carried to Babylon.

quote.text: all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store unto this day, shall be carried into Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the LORD.

claim.text: He sent his envoys to Hezekiah after Hezekiah's illness.
Sargon says he drove Merodach-baladan out of Babylon after twelve years; Sennacherib says he defeated him in the plain of Kish and later made him flee by ship.

In the year Sargon took Assyria's throne, "In Nisan Merodach-baladan took his seat on the throne in Babylon". In his second year the king of Elam fought Sargon while Merodach-baladan, coming to help, "did not come in time for the battle". In his twelfth year Sargon marched on Akkad and Merodach-baladan "fled to Elam": "Merodach-baladan reigned twelve years in Babylon."
The list gives "Marduk-aplu-iddin" twelve years, and later, after two years of Sennacherib and one month of "Marduk-zakir-shum", a second "Marduk-aplu-iddin" reign of nine months.

"Merodach-baladan, son of Iakin, king of Chaldea … Twelve years he ruled and governed Babylon, the city of the lord of the gods, against the will of the gods"; when Sargon advanced he fled "from Babylon to the city of Ikbi-Bel … at night".

In his first campaign Sennacherib defeated "Merodach-baladan, king of Babylonia, together with the army of Elam, his ally, in the plain of Kish"; Merodach-baladan "forsook his camp and made his escape alone", and Sennacherib plundered his palace in Babylon. Later Merodach-baladan loaded his gods into ships "and fled like a bird" to a city in the sea.

first.text: Kings: "he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick".

second.text: Isaiah: "he had heard that he had been sick, and was recovered".

first.text: Kings: the king of Babylon sent letters and a present because of the sickness.

second.text: Chronicles: "the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon" came "to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land".

questions.question: When did his envoys come to Hezekiah?

argument.text: "At that time", when he heard Hezekiah had been sick and had recovered.

views.label: In his first reign, before Sargon drove him out

argument.text: Merodach-baladan held Babylon against Sargon from 722 BC and sent the embassy probably hoping for an alliance with Hezekiah, also an enemy of Sargon.

views.label: In his short second reign
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912); Ellicott's commentary, following Schrader

argument.text: Rogers: when he retook Babylon, "His first move was to send an embassy to Hezekiah"; Ellicott's commentary says "perhaps" it was then, during a brief reign of six months.

views.label: It depends on the date of the illness

argument.text: If Hezekiah's illness came before Sennacherib's invasion, the embassy belongs to the long first reign; if after, to the brief second one.

views.label: To greet him after his sickness

argument.text: "For he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick."
"To enquire of the wonder that was done in the land."

views.label: To seek an ally
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93), retelling the story; R. W. Rogers (1912); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Josephus says Baladan "desired he would be his ally and his friend"; Rogers judged that "the real motive was to stir up disaffection against Assyria".
Both books call him "the son of Baladan".
Sargon calls him "son of Iakini" and "son of Iakin, king of Chaldea".

views.label: "Son of Iakin" names his tribe, not his father

argument.text: Ellicott's commentary reads "son of Yâkin" as "territorial rather than genealogical", like "Jehu son of Omri", and notes that the cuneiform inscriptions do not give his father's name.

notSaid: Scripture says nothing of Merodach-baladan's wars with Assyria or of how long he reigned.
Scripture does not say what answer the envoys took back to Babylon.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where his envoys came to Hezekiah

rulers.name: Nebuchadnezzar
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.tagline: The king of Babylon who took Jerusalem, burned the temple and carried Judah into exile; Daniel's king.

capital.name: Babylon
capital.note: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built"

identifications.text: Ezekiel always, and Jeremiah mostly, spell his name Nebuchadrezzar; Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther and Daniel spell it Nebuchadnezzar, as Jeremiah does in chapters 27–29 and at 34:1 and 39:5.

Scripture does not name his father. His own building inscription begins "Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, … son of Nabopolassar, king of Babylon, am I"; Berosus, quoted by Josephus, also makes him Nabopolassar's son.

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign. It dates events by his years, from his first to his twenty-third.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: His first year = Jehoiakim's fourth (Jer 25:1); Jehoiachin taken in his eighth (2 Kgs 24:12); Zedekiah's tenth = his eighteenth (Jer 32:1); the temple burned in his nineteenth (2 Kgs 25:8); deportations in his 7th, 18th and 23rd (Jer 52:28–30).

dates.label: Rogers (1912)
dates.note: Ptolemy's canon gives him 43 years from 604 BC; Berosus also gives 43 years.

dates.label: Babylonian Chronicle 5
dates.note: Crown prince at Carchemish in 605 BC; on his father's death he returned and took the throne the same year (Wiseman's edition, facts only).

scriptureSays.text: The LORD calls him "Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant", and says "have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar".
Daniel to the king: "Thou, O king, art a king of kings: for the God of heaven hath given thee a kingdom, power, and strength, and glory"; "Thou art this head of gold."
Ezra 5:12: God "gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house, and carried the people away into Babylon".
Daniel 5 recalls that "when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne", till he knew that the most high God ruled.
His own last words in Daniel: "Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven … and those that walk in pride he is able to abase."

quote.text: in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon
and the king of Babylon took him in the eighth year of his reign
in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar

claim.text: He smote the army of Pharaoh-necho at Carchemish by the Euphrates "in the fourth year of Jehoiakim", the year Jeremiah 25:1 calls his own first.

Daniel dates a siege of Jerusalem to Jehoiakim's third year: the Lord gave Jehoiakim into his hand with part of the temple vessels, and the king had young men of Israel, of the king's seed and of the princes, Daniel among them, brought to be taught the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.

events.label: The dream of the great image

claim.text: In his second year he dreamed of an image of gold, silver, brass, iron and clay, struck by a stone "cut out without hands"; Daniel told the dream and its meaning.
Jehoiakim became his servant three years, then rebelled; the LORD sent bands of Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites against Judah.
"The king of Egypt came not again any more out of his land: for the king of Babylon had taken from the river of Egypt unto the river Euphrates all that pertained to the king of Egypt."
Chronicles: he bound Jehoiakim in fetters to carry him to Babylon, and took temple vessels to his temple there.
"In the seventh year three thousand Jews and three and twenty."
He came against Jerusalem; Jehoiachin went out to him and was taken "in the eighth year of his reign", with the temple treasures, 10,000 captives, and the craftsmen and smiths.
He made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king and changed his name to Zedekiah; Chronicles says he "had made him swear by God".
In Zedekiah's ninth year, tenth month, tenth day, he came with all his host against Jerusalem and built forts round about it.
"In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty and two persons."
Zedekiah was overtaken in the plains of Jericho and brought to him at Riblah; his sons were slain before his eyes, his eyes put out, and he was carried to Babylon in fetters.
In his nineteenth year Nebuzar-adan, captain of the guard, burned the house of the LORD, the king's house and all the houses of Jerusalem, and broke down its walls.
He charged Nebuzar-adan: "Take him, and look well to him, and do him no harm".
Over the people left in Judah he made Gedaliah son of Ahikam ruler.
"In the three and twentieth year of Nebuchadrezzar Nebuzar-adan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty and five persons."
Ezekiel says he "caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus", and "yet had he no wages".

events.label: The golden image and the furnace

claim.text: He set up an image of gold sixty cubits high in the plain of Dura; Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego would not worship it and were cast into the furnace, and came out unhurt.
He dreamed of a great tree hewn down, its stump left "till seven times pass over him"; Daniel said the tree was the king.

Twelve months later, boasting over "great Babylon", he was driven from men and ate grass as oxen, until his understanding returned and he blessed the most High; he was established again in his kingdom.

worship.text: He put the temple vessels in "the house of his god"; Cyrus later brought them out.
His decree: anyone who spoke amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego would be cut in pieces, "because there is no other God that can deliver after this sort".
He sent a letter "unto all people, nations, and languages" telling "the signs and wonders that the high God hath wrought toward me".

building.text: "Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power".

alliances.text: Jehoiakim served him three years, then rebelled.
Jeremiah told Zedekiah: "Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and live."
Zedekiah rebelled against him, "who had made him swear by God".

people.text: He carried away Jerusalem's princes, mighty men, craftsmen and smiths; "none remained, save the poorest sort of the people of the land".
Jeremiah 52 counts 4,600 persons carried away in his 7th, 18th and 23rd years; Kings gives 10,000 for the first deportation alone.
He made Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon and set Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego over its affairs.
Ezra and Nehemiah list "the children of the province" whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away, who came back.

claim.text: Jeremiah called him the LORD's servant, told Judah and the nations to serve him, foretold that he would take Jerusalem and come against Egypt, and later said that, after the king of Assyria, "this Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon hath broken his bones".

quote.text: And now have I given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant

claim.text: Ezekiel foretold his siege of Tyre, and said that because his army served against Tyre without wages, Egypt would be given him "for his labour".

quote.text: Behold, I will give the land of Egypt unto Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon

claim.text: Daniel told and interpreted his two dreams, and counselled him: "break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor".

quote.text: Thou art this head of gold.

claim.text: A prophet who said, against Jeremiah, that the LORD would break Nebuchadnezzar's yoke within two years.

quote.text: Even so will I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all nations within the space of two full years.

claim.text: Jehoiakim served him, Jehoiachin surrendered to him, Zedekiah was made king by him and rebelled, and Gedaliah was set over those left in the land.
He smote Pharaoh-necho's army at Carchemish; Jeremiah foretold Pharaoh-hophra's fall "as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar".
Ezekiel foretold his siege of Tyre; Jeremiah his blow against Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor.

The chronicle records that in 605 BC crown prince Nebuchadnezzar beat the Egyptian army at Carchemish and destroyed its remnant in the district of Hamath, then returned to take the throne; that in his seventh year he besieged the city of Judah, took it on the second of Adar (16 March 597 BC on Wiseman's reckoning), seized its king and appointed a king of his own choosing. It names no king of Judah, and it stops in 594 BC, before the burning of the temple.
Administrative tablets from his palace stores list oil rations for Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahudu (Jehoiachin) and for five sons of the king of Judah.

outside.name: Tablet of his campaign against Egypt

claim.text: A broken tablet reads: "In the thirty-seventh year of Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, [the kings of] Egypt came up to do battle and Amasis, king of Egypt called out his troops". The rest is too damaged to tell the outcome.

Most of his inscriptions describe building rather than war. One begins "Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, preserver of Esagila and Ezida, son of Nabopolassar" and tells of a great new wall for Babylon, "that which no king before me had done, I did".

outside.name: Berosus, quoted by Josephus
outside.date: Berosus wrote about 290 BC; Josephus about AD 95

claim.text: Berosus says that Nebuchadnezzar, sent as a young man against the rebel governor of Egypt and Phoenicia, heard of his father's death, hurried to Babylon across the desert and took the kingdom; that he rebuilt Babylon with three walls round the inner and outer city and built a new palace with a "pensile paradise" for his Median queen; and that he "fell sick, and departed this life, when he had reigned forty-three years".

outside.name: The records of Tyre, quoted by Josephus

claim.text: Josephus quotes the Phoenician records: "Nabuchodonosor besieged Tyre for thirteen years in the days of Ithobal, their king".

first.text: Kings: "So Jehoiakim slept with his fathers".

second.text: Chronicles: Nebuchadnezzar "bound him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon".

first.text: Kings: in "the eighth year of his reign", "ten thousand captives".

second.text: Jeremiah 52: "in the seventh year three thousand Jews and three and twenty".

first.text: Kings: the fifth month, "on the seventh day of the month", his nineteenth year.

second.text: Jeremiah 52: the fifth month, "in the tenth day of the month", his nineteenth year.

first.text: Kings: the king of Babylon took him "in the eighth year of his reign".

second.text: Chronicles: "when the year was expired, king Nebuchadnezzar sent, and brought him to Babylon".

questions.question: Did he come against Jerusalem in Jehoiakim's third year or fourth?

argument.text: Daniel: "In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim … came Nebuchadnezzar". Jeremiah: Jehoiakim's fourth year "was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar", the year of Carchemish.

views.label: "Came" means set out
views.holders: E. W. Hengstenberg, C. F. Keil and O. Zöckler (as reported by S. R. Driver, 1900); Ellicott's commentary

argument.text: The word "came" marks the starting point: Nebuchadnezzar set out from Babylon in Jehoiakim's third year and reached Judah after Carchemish in the fourth.

views.label: The end of the third, the start of the fourth

argument.text: Gill places the event at the close of Jehoiakim's third year and the beginning of the fourth, "which was the first of Nebuchadnezzar".
Driver held the date historically doubtful: it rests on a tradition also found in 2 Chronicles 36:6–7, and the invasion of 2 Kings 24:1 belongs after Jehoiakim's fourth year.

questions.question: Do records outside the Bible speak of his madness (Daniel 4)?

argument.text: He was driven from men, ate grass as oxen, and his hair grew like eagles' feathers; the decree had said "till seven times pass over him". Then his understanding returned.
Josephus retells Daniel: the king lived in the desert seven years, and no one dared seize his kingdom. He adds no other source.

Berosus says only that he "fell sick, and departed this life". Ellicott's commentary says nothing of this sickness is recorded by Berosus "unless the vague statement … be pressed"; Driver judged it too vague to confirm Daniel, since it is a sickness he died of.

views.label: A rare illness, as described
views.holders: E. B. Pusey (1864), as reported by S. R. Driver (1900); Ellicott's commentary

argument.text: The malady matches the rare disorder called lycanthropy, in which a sufferer believes himself an animal; Driver adds that, were the book the work of a contemporary, he saw no sufficient reason to doubt the account.

views.label: An echo in a Babylonian legend
views.holders: Abydenus (probably 2nd century AD, quoted by Eusebius); A. A. Bevan, as quoted by S. R. Driver (1900)

argument.text: Abydenus reports a Chaldean story that Nebuchadnezzar went up on his palace roof and, "possessed by some god", foretold the Persian conquest and wished that the conqueror might be "driven through the desert, where … wild beasts have their pasture", then vanished. Bevan judged the resemblance to Daniel 4 not accidental and the legend the more primitive.

views.label: A memory of Nabonidus
views.holders: H. de Genouillac (1925), as reported by R. P. Dougherty (1929)

argument.text: Genouillac suggested that the madness and life among wild beasts reflect the last king, Nabonidus, and his years at Tema in Arabia. Dougherty reports that Baumgartner criticised this and calls it "extremely hypothetical".

notSaid: Scripture does not say how long Nebuchadnezzar reigned or how he died.
Scripture does not name his father.
Daniel does not say how long "seven times" is.
Scripture does not say whether his campaign against Egypt took place as Jeremiah and Ezekiel foretold it.

places.name: Tahpanhes
places.note: Where Jeremiah hid the stones for his throne

rulers.name: Evil-merodach
rulers.title: King of Babylon
rulers.tagline: The king of Babylon who brought Jehoiachin out of prison and fed him at his table.

identifications.text: Scripture does not name his father. Berosus, quoted by Josephus, calls him Nebuchadnezzar's son; Rogers (1912) gives his Babylonian name as Amel-Marduk, "Man (servant) of Marduk".

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign. It dates his release of Jehoiachin to the year he began to reign, the 37th of Jehoiachin's captivity.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: "In the year that he began to reign" (2 Kgs 25:27), "in the first year of his reign" (Jer 52:31): the 37th year of Jehoiachin's captivity.

dates.label: Rogers (1912)
dates.note: Ptolemy's canon: two years from 561 BC.

dates.label: Berosus and Josephus
dates.note: Berosus (quoted by Josephus) gives two years; Josephus's own Antiquities gives eighteen.

scriptureSays.text: "Evil-merodach king of Babylon in the year that he began to reign did lift up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison".
"He spake kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon".
Jehoiachin changed his prison garments and ate bread before him "all the days of his life", with a daily allowance from the king.

quote.text: in the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah

claim.text: In the first year of his reign he brought Jehoiachin out of prison and spoke kindly to him.

events.label: A throne above the other kings

claim.text: He set Jehoiachin's throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon.
Jehoiachin ate at the king's table, with "a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life".

alliances.text: Other captive kings were kept in Babylon with Jehoiachin; Jehoiachin's throne was set above theirs.

people.text: Judah's captive king was given new garments and a place at the king's table.

claim.text: He released Jehoiachin in the 37th year of his captivity.
Nebuchadnezzar had carried Jehoiachin to Babylon; Evil-merodach brought him "out of prison".

"His son Evilmerodach obtained the kingdom. He governed public affairs after an illegal and impure manner, and had a plot laid against him by Neriglissoor, his sister's husband, and was slain by him when he had reigned but two years."
Amel-Marduk, two years, from 561 BC in Rogers's table of the canon.

Josephus says Evil-Merodach "immediately set Jeconiah at liberty, and esteemed him among his most intimate friends", because his father "had not kept his faith with Jeconiah"; he gives him a reign of eighteen years.
Some thirty years earlier, palace tablets of Nebuchadnezzar's reign already list oil rations for Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahudu (Jehoiachin). They say nothing of a prison, or of his release.

first.text: Kings: the twelfth month, "on the seven and twentieth day of the month".

second.text: Jeremiah 52: the twelfth month, "in the five and twentieth day of the month".

first.text: Kings: "in the year that he began to reign".

second.text: Jeremiah 52: "in the first year of his reign".

views.label: Two years
views.holders: Berosus (quoted by Josephus); Ptolemy's canon; R. P. Dougherty (1929)

argument.text: Berosus: slain "when he had reigned but two years"; Ptolemy's canon also gives two years; Dougherty, from the cuneiform texts, gives 562–560 BC.
In the Antiquities Josephus gives Evil-Merodach a reign of eighteen years; Dougherty calls this chronology inaccurate.

notSaid: Scripture does not say why he released Jehoiachin.
Scripture does not call him Nebuchadnezzar's son, and does not say how his reign ended.
Scripture does not say how long Jehoiachin lived after his release.

rulers.name: Belshazzar
rulers.title: King of Babylon, as Daniel calls him
rulers.tagline: The king at whose feast the writing appeared on the wall; slain the same night.

identifications.text: Daniel calls Nebuchadnezzar his father (Daniel 5:2, 11, 13, 18, 22), and the site's person record lists Nebuchadnezzar as his parent on that basis. The Babylonian inscriptions name Nabonidus as his father; the views are set out below.

He is the Bel-shar-usur of the Babylonian inscriptions, for whom Nabonidus prays as "the first-born son, the issue of my body". Rogers (1912) and Wilson (1915) hold the identification; Josephus, writing earlier, took Belshazzar to be Nabonidus himself (see below).

reign.text: Scripture gives no length for his reign. Daniel dates visions to his first and third years.

dates.label: Dougherty (1929): kingship entrusted to him
dates.note: Entrusted with the kingship in Nabonidus's third year (553 BC) and acting as co-regent, on Dougherty's view, until Babylon fell in 539.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: Daniel 7:1 is dated "in the first year of Belshazzar" and Daniel 8:1 "in the third year"; Scripture gives no length.

dates.label: Nabonidus, his father (Dougherty 1929)
dates.note: Nabonidus's reign: 17 years.

dates.label: Driver (1900)
dates.note: Nabonidus's reign; Driver held that Belshazzar was "the king's son", not king.

scriptureSays.text: "Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords", and had the gold and silver vessels from the temple at Jerusalem brought in to drink from.
Daniel to the king: "thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this".
"TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting."
"In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain."

events.label: The feast and the temple vessels

claim.text: At a feast for a thousand lords the king, his princes, wives and concubines drank from the vessels taken from the temple at Jerusalem and "praised the gods of gold, and of silver".
Fingers of a man's hand wrote on the plaister of the palace wall; the king's wise men could not read it.
The queen told him of Daniel, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made master of the magicians.
Daniel read MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN: the kingdom numbered and finished, the king weighed and found wanting, the kingdom "given to the Medes and Persians".
Daniel was clothed with scarlet and proclaimed "the third ruler in the kingdom".
"In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. And Darius the Median took the kingdom".
In his first year Daniel saw four great beasts come up from the sea.

events.label: The vision of the ram and the goat

claim.text: In his third year Daniel, in vision at Shushan by the river Ulai, saw the ram and the he goat.

worship.text: The vessels of the house of God were used at his feast while the gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood and stone were praised.

alliances.text: Daniel: "Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians."

people.text: He made Daniel, "of the children of the captivity of Judah", the third ruler in the kingdom.

claim.text: Daniel told the king to keep his gifts, reminded him how Nebuchadnezzar had been humbled, and read the writing as the end of his kingdom. Daniel 7 and 8 are dated by his years.

quote.text: TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.

claim.text: "Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old."
Daniel 5 speaks of Nebuchadnezzar as his father, whose humbling he knew of.
Nabonidus ends a prayer to the moon god: "And as for Belshazzar, the first-born son, the issue of my body, do thou implant in his heart the fear of thy great divinity" (Rogers's translation).
Before leaving for Tema in Arabia, Nabonidus "entrusted a camp to his eldest, firstborn son … He freed his hand; he entrusted the kingship to him" (Dougherty's translation).

For several years the chronicle says the king stayed in Tema while "the king's son" was with the army in Akkad; Rogers and Driver both take the king's son to be Belshazzar. It records that Babylon was taken by Ugbaru (Gobryas) and that Cyrus entered the city on the third of Marchesvan; Nabonidus was taken in the city. A damaged line about a death is read in different ways (see below).

Herodotus calls the last king "Labynetos", son of a Labynetos and of queen Nitocris, and says that when the Persians entered Babylon those in the middle of the city, "as they chanced to be holding a festival, they went on dancing and rejoicing" until they learned the truth.

Xenophon tells how Cyrus heard that it was "a time of high festival in Babylon when the citizens drink and make merry the whole night long", sent his men in by the dry river bed, and how Gobryas and Gadatas forced the palace and found the king "on his feet, with his drawn scimitar" and overwhelmed him. Xenophon does not name the king.
Berosus says the last king, "Nabonnedus", was beaten in battle, shut himself in Borsippa and surrendered to Cyrus, who sent him to live in Carmania. He does not mention Belshazzar.

argument.text: The queen speaks of "the king Nebuchadnezzar thy father", and Daniel says "thou his son, O Belshazzar".

views.label: "Father" means grandfather
views.holders: the Geneva Bible notes (1599); Matthew Poole (1683–85); Joseph Benson (1811–18)

argument.text: The Geneva note on Daniel 5:2: "Meaning his grandfather". Poole says he "might be called his son though his grandson", citing Jeremiah 27:7 ("him, and his son, and his son's son"); Benson makes him the son of Evil-merodach.

views.label: Son of Nabonidus, by the inscriptions
views.holders: the Babylonian inscriptions; R. W. Rogers (1912)

argument.text: Nabonidus calls Belshazzar "the first-born son, the issue of my body".

views.label: Nebuchadnezzar's grandson through his mother
views.holders: R. P. Dougherty (1929); allowed as a possibility by S. R. Driver (1900)

argument.text: Dougherty argued, from a chain of circumstantial evidence, that Nabonidus's wife Nitocris was a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar, so that Belshazzar was Nebuchadnezzar's grandson. Driver allowed the possibility, but noted that no inscription of Nabonidus implies any tie to Nebuchadnezzar, and that Daniel 5 gives the "impression that in the view of the writer Belshazzar was actually Nebuchadnezzar's son".
Wilson: either one was his real and the other his adoptive father, or the greatest of his predecessors is called his father, "just as Omri is called by the Assyrians the father of Jehu".
Josephus says the kingdom came to "Baltasar, who by the Babylonians was called Naboandelus", and that Babylon was taken "when he had reigned seventeen years".
"Belshazzar the king"; "the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon"; "the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar".

Driver: the inscriptions call him regularly "the king's son", to the day of his death, and "lend no support" to his being his father's viceroy; a co-regency, he wrote, was "destitute of foundation in the inscriptions".

views.label: He ruled in his father's name
views.holders: R. W. Rogers (1912); R. D. Wilson (1915)

argument.text: Rogers: while Nabonidus lived in Tema, state affairs and the army "had all fallen into the hands of the king's son, Belshazzar … who ruled in his father's name". Wilson held that a crown prince acting as sub-king could be called king of Babylon.

Dougherty, using the Verse Account published in 1924 ("he entrusted the kingship to him"), held that Belshazzar was co-regent from 553 BC and that there was no positive evidence the arrangement ended before Babylon fell.

questions.question: What does "the third ruler in the kingdom" mean?

views.label: Third after Nabonidus and Belshazzar
views.holders: Hugo Grotius (first suggested it, according to Dougherty); R. P. Dougherty (1929)

argument.text: With Nabonidus first and Belshazzar second, the highest reward left to give was third place.
Driver summarises verse 29 as Daniel being made "one of the three chief ministers of the kingdom".

views.label: A title of rank
views.holders: C. C. Torrey, as reported by R. P. Dougherty (1929)

argument.text: Torrey took the phrase as a rank: the interpreter "shall govern the kingdom as third ruler".

views.label: A third part of the kingdom

argument.text: Josephus has the king promise "the third part of his own dominions".

questions.question: Does the Nabonidus Chronicle record Belshazzar's death?

views.label: Yes: "he killed the son of the king"
views.holders: H. Hagen (1894), accepted by T. G. Pinches; followed by S. R. Driver (1900) and R. D. Wilson (1915)

argument.text: Hagen read a damaged line as "and he killed the son of the king". Driver, following this reading, wrote that the "king's son" was slain in the night, eight days after Cyrus entered Babylon; Wilson also took the son of the king to be Belshazzar.

views.label: No: "the wife of the king died"
views.holders: H. Winckler (1889); E. Schrader (1890); Sidney Smith (1924), as reported by R. P. Dougherty (1929)

argument.text: These scholars read the same line as the death of the king's wife; Smith, who made the latest copy, called Hagen's reading "impossible".

Dougherty examined the tablet and found the traces "not sufficiently legible for decisive conclusion", though he thought the circumstances favoured the reading "the wife of the king"; Daniel 5 and Xenophon both place the king's death at the capture of the city.

notSaid: Daniel does not name Nabonidus.
Scripture does not say who killed Belshazzar or how.
Scripture gives no length for his reign.
